description: Somos un equipo de investigación multidisciplinario representando la ciudad de Chimbote en Perú, para abordar los mayores desafíos legales, médicos, tecnológicos y sociales de la exploración espacial y el establecimiento de asentamientos en la Luna y Marte.
summary: We developed YupizaEduca, an atlas that utilizes orbital data to characterize hyper-arid and volcanic terrestrial environments as analogs for future lunar and Martian bases. Drawing on NASA observations, the system cross-references variables—such as toxic mineral content, ultraviolet radiation, and atmospheric pressure—with thresholds for cardiopulmonary and ocular pathologies, non-invasive salivary biomarkers, and planetary protection regulations (COSPAR and the Artemis Accords). Its value proposition lies in translating complex geospatial data into a multidisciplinary "risk traffic-light" system that simultaneously assesses the clinical safety of a crew and the legal viability of a given site. Through a no-code platform that integrates diagnostic polygons (via Felt) and orbital comparison tools (via ArcGIS), the project provides space agencies, field researchers, and policymakers with a scalable, preventive framework to safeguard human health and planetary ecological integrity prior to launch.
details:
YupizaEduca: Orbital remote sensing of hyper-arid and volcanic analogs for dust toxicology, salivary biomarkers, and planetary protection law.

1. What is YupizaEduca and how does it work?

It is an interactive digital space that utilizes NASA orbital observations of hyperarid and volcanic environments on Earth as analogues for future lunar and Martian bases. Unlike traditional maps, the platform crossreferences critical environmental data such as toxic mineral content, ultraviolet radiation, and atmospheric pressure with medical thresholds for cardiopulmonary and ocular pathologies, protocols for noninvasive salivary biomarkers, and considerations regarding space law. All of this is synthesized into a "Multidisciplinary Risk Traffic Light" system, developed using diagnostic polygons in Felt and orbital comparison tools in ArcGIS, providing space agencies, researchers, and policymakers with a preventive tool to be used prior to any crewed deployment. Its operation is structured around three main pillars:

  • Orbital and Environmental Layer: Satellite monitoring of heavy metal concentrations and toxic mining waste, ultraviolet (UV) radiation indices, and atmospheric pressure gradients in hyperarid and volcanic zones.
  • Biomedical and Non-Invasive Monitoring Layer: Directly correlates environmental variables with clinical risk thresholds for cardiopulmonary and ocular health. It incorporates monitoring protocols based on non-invasive salivary biomarkers (cortisol, immunoglobulin A, inflammatory markers) to detect early physiological stress without the need for complex procedures in the field.
  • Legal/Juridical Layer: Automated assessment of a site’s legal viability based on COSPAR planetary protection categories (prevention of forward and backward biological contamination) and the guidelines of the Artemis Accords (sustainable use of resources, safety zones, and heritage protection).

2. A benefit to humanity

The interactive digital space features a preventive and immediate risk-assessment system modeled like a traffic light that makes it possible to evaluate whether a site is safe for human life and legally viable before beginning any deployment or mission.

Its key benefits are divided into five strategic areas:

  • Non-invasive clinical prevention:
    Protects the cardiopulmonary and ocular health of crews against extreme UV
    radiation, low atmospheric pressure, and toxic mining dust, by incorporating
    salivary biomarkers that detect physiological stress without the need for blood draws or hospital grade equipment in the field.
  • Regulatory compliance and planetary protection: Ensure, from the planning phase onward, that operations adhere to COSPAR’s biological contamination prevention categories and the sustainable use principles of the Artemis Accords, thereby mitigating legal and environmental risks.
  • Time and operational cost savings: It consolidates within a single visual tool information that is typically analyzed separately by geologists, aerospace physicians, and legal specialists, thereby accelerating the selection and validation of analog sites on Earth.
  • Easily accessible and intuitive (No-Code): By operating on diagnostic polygons in Felt and orbital comparators in ArcGIS, it eliminates technical programming barriers and facilitates direct collaboration among multidisciplinary teams.
  • Specific impact depending on the profile whether a lawyer, a doctor, or a field researcher.

3. Characteristics that define the future

In the future, its impact will transform science and health on three very clear fronts:

  • It will serve as a mandatory prerequisite before liftoff: it will become the foundational certification for agencies and universities prior to conducting training in deserts or on volcanoes helping to prevent medical emergencies and ensuring that every mission complies with space laws from day one.
  • It will serve as a shield for astronauts on the Moon and Mars: our data will help calculate how long an astronaut can venture outside their base without sustaining damage to their lungs or eyes from toxic dust and radiation, while allowing for rapid health monitoring via a simple saliva sample.
  • It will be the system that protects astronauts, while also serving to safeguard the health of workers and communities in terrestrial mining areas. Furthermore, since it requires no programming, any university or emerging nation will be able to conduct top tier space science without the need for expensive supercomputers.

With YupizaEduca, we will make space exploration safer, more legal, and more accessible for everyone.

 

4. No-code tools used

Felt was used for the diagnostic polygons, while ArcGIS along with satellite data and orbital observations from NASA was employed for orbital comparisons. Additionally, clinical biotechnology and non-invasive monitoring methods were utilized, as were the regulatory frameworks and planetary laws referenced in the Artemis Accords and the COSPAR planetary protection policies.

5. Innovation as an advantage

What makes it unique is that, for the first time, it brings together three worlds that previously operated separately NASA satellites, preventive medicine, and space law within a platform as intuitive as a traffic light. Its innovation can be summarized by three key advantages:

  • An intelligent traffic light with an "emergency brake": We don’t just display maps of rocks; we translate complex data into Green, Yellow, or Red. For instance, if a piece of terrain resembles Mars but conceals toxic mining waste or violates an international treaty, the system triggers a critical veto and halts the mission instantly.
  • From space to a drop of saliva and the legal framework: We connect radiation and dust observed from orbit with rapid, painless saliva tests (to monitor stress and immunity without the need to set up hospitals in the desert), while simultaneously verifying on the ground that planetary protection rules (COSPAR and the Artemis Accords) are being followed.
  • Zero programming and easy to use: Since it operates within Felt and ArcGIS without requiring a single line of code, any doctor, lawyer, or scientist can use it today whether to protect future astronauts on the Moon, or to safeguard mining workers and communities here on Earth.

6. What factors did the team consider during development?

It was conceived very much like a real mission: it is not enough for a site to simply resemble Mars it must also be safe for life and legally viable. For this reason, our team built the platform around four key factors:

  • The extreme reality of fieldwork: We know that you cannot set up a clinical laboratory in the middle of a desert or on a volcano. That is why we opted for rapid saliva tests rather than invasive procedures, linking them to NASA satellites to protect the crew’s lungs and eyes from UV radiation, low pressure, and toxic dust.
  • Zero tolerance for hidden risks: In space exploration, a single error costs lives. We have designed an automatic veto system to ensure that no site is approved even if its geology is identical to that of the Moon if it harbors toxic mining waste or health hazards.
  • Legal safeguards from day one: We integrate international treaties (COSPAR and the Artemis Accords) directly into our maps to prevent a mission from being halted due to non compliance with environmental or planetary protection standards.
  • Zero technical barriers for decisión makers: We know that medical professionals, policymakers, and mission directors need answers, not complex code. We rely on a 100% no-code platform (Felt and ArcGIS) so that anyone can evaluate a site in seconds.

YupizaEduca spans from orbit to the clinic and the law, evaluating human safety and legal viability before liftoff toward the Moon and Mars.
